We find that companies with better ESG performance tend to have a higher propensity to choose the Greenfield investment mode for OFDI, and this conclusion remains robust across various robustness tests and adjustments for endogeneity. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the higher the performance level of ESG in the host country, when there is no bilateral investment agreement, investment sensitive industries and high intangible assets enterprises, the effect of improving ESG performance to promote enterprises' choice of green space Sinvestment mode is more significant. Introduction I T R OFDI is a key strategy for firms to enhance their international competitiveness and A efficiently utilize global resources. By increasing OFDI, firms in developing countries can not only promote their own scale expansion and technological innovation (Hong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019),but also foster greater connectivity between developing and developed countries, jointly promoting global economic growth (Giroud & Ivarsson, 2020). Therefore, exploring how to promote the OFDI strategies of firms in developing countries is of critical importance. According to Dunning (2001), the three most important factors for corporate to OFDI are ownership, location and internalization advantages. Compared with companies in developed countries, firms in developing countries have smaller ownership advantages and face greater legitimacy issues and survival pressures in the host country's market (Dunning et al., 2008). Compared with foreign firms that possess advantages such as advanced technology, capital reserves, and skilled employees, companies in developing countries often face more severe 'liability of foreignness' ARTICLE IN PRESS issues in areas such as environmental governance, social responsibility, and internal management (Abid & Sekrafi, 2021). In recent years, the concept of ESG has emerged and evolved, advocating for companies to integrate environmental, social, and governance factors into their business philosophy and long-term development strategies. An increasing number of institutional investors are incorporating ESG performance into their investment decisions (Wei &Wu, 2024). ESG integrates environmental, social, and ethical value standards, and its core is broader than traditional concepts (Gillan et al., 2021). The ESG development concept requires companies not only to pursue economic value but also to take into account social and environmental responsibilities. The ESG development concept has become one of the viable paths to enhance the brand recognition of companies in developing countries and Salleviate the 'liability of foreignness' in overseas investment (Wang et al., 2024). S E The development of the ESG concept has led to a profound change in the R competitive logic of companies and their OFDI decision-making, prompting scholars P to rethink how corporate ESG performance in fluences OFDI strategies. Many scholars N believe that enhancements in ESG performance can promote corporate OFDI (Wang et I al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023). The reaso ns for this include the fact that ESG performance E can alleviate corporate financingL constraints (Zhang & Lucey, 2022), enhance corporate C reputation (Yang et al., 2023), accelerate digital transformation and technological I innovation (Li & Li, 2024), and strengthen the company's internationalization T advantages (Tang Ret al., 2020), thereby enhancing companies' capabilities and A willingness to expand globally (Wang et al., 2024). The previous research on the impact of corporate ESG performance on OFDI has primarily focused on its effects on the willingness, scale, or overall returns of OFDI in international markets, with limited exploration of how ESG performance influences the mode of OFDI. Corporate OFDI modes typically include Greenfield Investment (GFI) and Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) , each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Mode selection is a crucial component of corporate OFDI strategy (Giachetti et al., 2019). Once the OFDI mode decision is implemented, it is difficult to reverse in the short term and entails high costs (Morschett et al., 2010). Different forms of cross- border investments can lead to markedly different economic outcomes. Therefore, an in-depth exploration of how ESG influences corporate OFDI mode selection, and examining the mechanisms through which ESG performance affects OFDI mode choice from a productivity perspective, will not only help companies from ARTICLE IN PRESS various countries select the appropriate mode for international expansion while enhancing their internal ESG capabilities but also integrate ESG as new competitive advantage into classical international investment theory, thereby further expanding and enriching the theory of corporate international investment. The literature most closely related to this study is Takayama (2021). Takayama, approaching from the perspective of corporate intangible assets, points out that the abundance of intangible capital is a crucial factor in determining investment models. Firms endowed with high intangible capital are more inclined to enter host countries through the greenfield mode, as they can mitigate the risk of technology spillover and maximize the synergistic effects of intangible assets through internalization. Conversely, firms lacking intangible capital tend to rely more on M&A to acquire complementary assets from domestic companies in the hoSst country. Notably, ESG performance serves as a concentrated manifestation andS core component of corporate E intangible assets and is intrinsically linked with intangible capital. As indicated by the R findings of this study, firms with superior ESG performance are significantly more P likely to engage in cross-border investment th rough the greenfield mode, corroborating N Takayama's intangible capital theory. I This research advances the theo retical framework and perspective initiated by E Takayama (2021). In TakayamLa's framework, intangible assets and productivity are C treated as parallel independent variables, each influencing a firm's foreign direct I investment models independently, without delving into the interlinked mechanisms T between the two. InR contrast, the key innovation of this study lies in integrating ESG A within Dunning's (2001) OLI model framework and Nocke & Yeaple's (2007) heterogeneous firm theory framework to construct an “ESG-OLI-TFP” transmission chain. This demonstrates the pathway through which ESG influences a firm's total factor productivity (TFP). ESG development can strengthen firms' ownership, locational, and internalization advantages, becoming a vital component of corporate intangible assets, thereby effectively enhancing firm TFP. Specifically, through pathways like optimizing resource allocation efficiency, enhancing innovation capability, and improving stakeholder relationships, ESG practices systematically bolster firms' OLI advantages and elevate productivity levels. This productivity boost further influences firms' preferences between cross-border M&A and GFI. This theoretical integration overcomes the limitations of prior studies, which have analyzed intangible assets and productivity in isolation, and reveals the intrinsic logic by which ESG affects investment model choices through its impact on productivity. It provides a ARTICLE IN PRESS more dynamic and systemic analytical perspective for understanding firms' international strategic decision-making. 2. This conclusion aligns with the heterogeneous firm trade theory proposed by Helpman et al. By distinguishing between intangible asset-intensive industries and traditional industries, the author validated the theoretical predictions of Nocke & Yeaple (2007). The choice of different market entry modes (export, greenfield outward direct investment, and cross-border mergers and acquisitions) by enterprises depends on the essential characteristics of enterprise heterogeneity, especially the proportion of intangible assets. Mallin et al. (2014) found that multinational companies that actively take on social S responsibility can enhance their reputation and mitigate the doubts of host country. At S the same time, host country governments are more wEilling to offer tax incentives to multinational companies that prioritize social rResponsibility, helping them garner P political support in the host country (Kim et al., 2024), thus creating a unique strategic advantage that supports sustainable operaNtions abroad. By proactively participating in I social welfare activities, multinational companies can gain a high reputation and E recognition from social stakeholders, easing the legitimacy pressure related to corporate L social responsibility (Liu & Richards, 2019), which, in turn, facilitates better overseas C operations and long-term sIurvival. T The ESG performance advantage can substantially stimulate innovation R (Cherkasova & NAenuzhenko, 2022), thus increasing the company's overseas revenue. The ESG transformation's differentiated advantage and the alignment with the host country's market preferences are key factors in translating a company's ESG performance advantage into overseas operations (Wang et al., 2023). According to Wang et al. (2024) , ESG performance can enhance a company's reputation, thereby expanding the scale of its OFDI. Overall, impact studies that currently focus solely on ESG or OFDI are relatively mature. However, research on the impact of ESG performance on corporate OFDI is still in its infancy, with considerable room and value for further development. There is still some research that remains insufficient and can be expanded upon. At the same time, most existing research on the impact of ESG performance on corporate OFDI focuses on the scale and scope of investment, and the few quantitative studies are mostly simple empirical regressions, lacking theoretical modeling and targeted research on the impact of ESG performance on corporate OFDI mode selection. However, it strictly relies on the continuity and non-negativity of investment data, which can lead to sample loss and estimation bias when there are numerous zero-investment firms in the sample. This reduces reliance on investment data, broadens the applicable sample range, and better captures short-term productivity fluctuations. However, the choice of intermediate inputs might be influenced by industry characteristics, and it still cannot fully avoid estimation errors caused by factor price distortions. The FE method, a fundamental panel data model approach, controls for individual effects that do not vary over time, partially eliminating omitted variable bias. It offers simplicity in model specification and low computational costs. However, it assumes that productivity shocks are exogenous, failing to address the dynamic endogeneity issue between input factors and productivity. JSON: Name: esg_ofdi_mode_tfp Title: Causal analysis of the effect of firm ESG performance on OFDI entry-mode choice using panel discrete-choice models and mediation analysis via total factor productivity Short Hypothesis: An exogenous increase in a firm's ESG performance causally raises the probability that the firm selects Greenfield investment rather than cross-border M&A for outward FDI, and this effect is mediated by increases in the firm's total factor productivity. Related Work: Prior research links firm heterogeneity and productivity to entry-mode selection (heterogeneous-firm and OLI frameworks) and separately links ESG performance to firm outcomes such as financing, reputation, innovation, and OFDI propensity. Existing studies primarily address OFDI scale or binary internationalization decisions and treat intangible assets or productivity as parallel predictors of mode choice. Empirical work on ESG and OFDI often relies on simple regressions, single-country samples, single ESG sources, limited endogeneity controls, and lacks explicit theoretical integration of ESG into OLI/heterogeneous-firm models or rigorous mediation testing via TFP. Research gaps include (1) few studies quantifying causal impact of ESG on OFDI mode, (2) limited use of instrumental or propensity-score methods to address reverse causality and selection, (3) inconsistent ESG measurement and rating divergence, and (4) inadequate evaluation of the productivity-mediated mechanism and heterogeneous effects by host-country institutional context and industry. Abstract: This project tests whether firm-level ESG performance causally affects the choice of OFDI entry mode (Greenfield investment vs cross-border M&A) and whether total factor productivity (TFP) mediates that effect. We combine a formal ESG-OLI-TFP conceptual model with panel discrete-choice estimation on firm–host–year observations. Empirically we estimate panel logit/probit/ cloglog specifications with host, industry and year fixed effects; address endogeneity using multiple instruments (e.g., holdings by ESG-focused funds, firm environmental-attention textual indicators, and environmental subsidies) and generalized propensity-score weighting; and compute mediation via alternative TFP measures (LP, OP, FE) with bootstrap inference. We report robustness to alternative ESG sources, alternative MODE definitions, and heterogeneous subsamples (host-country ESG level, sensitive industries, intangible-asset intensity, BIT presence). The main contribution is an integrated causal and mechanism analysis showing whether and how ESG advantages translate into mode selection through productivity improvements, with implications for firm strategy and international investment theory. Experiments: Datasets: firm-level panel of Chinese A-share listed companies (2009–2021); OFDI mode labels from matched fDi Markets (greenfield) and SDC Global M&A (acquisitions); ESG ratings from SNSI (primary) plus SynTao, Wind, Bloomberg (robustness); control variables from CSMAR; host-country covariates from World Bank WDI; government subsidy and textual disclosures from annual reports and Wind text database. Preprocessing: exclude financial firms, ST/*ST/PT, exit-year affiliates; multiple imputation for missing; winsorize at 0.05/0.95; create binary MODE (1=GFI,0=M&A) and alternative MODE_50 (parent share>=50%). Baseline models: panel logit with host/industry/year fixed effects, clustered SE at firm. Robustness: panel fixed-effects linear probability, probit, cloglog, and Poisson pseudo-ML. Endogeneity tests: two-stage IV procedures using (i) count of holdings by ESG-focused funds, (ii) firm-level environmental-attention text score, (iii) log environmental subsidies; report first-stage F-statistics, Anderson LM, Cragg-Donald. Propensity adjustments: generalized propensity score matching (GPSM) with IPW, probit-GPS, kernel-GPS. Mediation (mechanism) tests: compute firm TFP via Levinsohn-Petrin (LP), Olley-Pakes (OP), and firm fixed-effects (FE); estimate (A) ESG→TFP (OLS/FE), (B) MODE on ESG and TFP and interaction terms (IV where applicable); compute mediated effect (product-of-coefs) with 1,000 bootstrap CIs and Sobel-type statistics; report proportion mediated. Evaluation metrics: marginal effects of ESG on MODE, ATE/ATT from GPSM, pseudo-R2, IV first-stage F, overidentification p-values, t-stats and p-values, bootstrap CI widths, mediation proportion and significance. Comparisons/ablations: (1) drop mediator (TFP) to compare direct effect; (2) single-instrument vs multiple-instrument IV estimates; (3) alternative ESG sources; (4) alternative MODE definitions; (5) restrict sample to OFDI-active firms; (6) placebo tests using lagged non-related firm attributes. Heterogeneity analyses: split-sample by host-country ESG index (high/low), presence/absence of bilateral investment treaty, OFDI-sensitive industries, and firm intangible-asset share. All regressions include robust standard errors clustered at firm and report sensitivity to different clustering and bootstrap seeds. Risk Factors and Limitations: Weak or invalid instruments (weak first-stage, violation of exclusion) may produce biased IV estimates; measurement error and rating divergence across ESG providers can attenuate coefficients or produce inconsistent inferences; reverse causality and omitted confounders may not be fully eliminated despite IV/PSM—especially if unobservables correlate with instruments; TFP estimation methods (LP/OP/FE) have method-specific biases (zero-investment, proxy selection, dynamic endogeneity) that affect mediation quantification; sample restricted to Chinese listed firms limits external validity to other institutional contexts; rare-event or selection bias if majority of firms do not undertake OFDI; database matching errors for mode labels (GFI vs M&A) can misclassify outcomes; computational and data constraints may limit bootstrap iterations or subgroup sample sizes for precise inference; heterogeneous regulatory or geopolitical shocks during the period could confound time-varying effects; causal estimates depend on functional-form choices (logit vs probit vs linear) and fixed-effect specifications.
